title: Dillard's vs. Nordstrom (in-class exercise)
stem:
From the S19 in-class exercise. Dillard's (rows) and Nordstrom (columns) each choose which clothing line to feature. Payoffs: (Dillard's, Nordstrom).

| Dillard's \ Nordstrom | Girl's | Women's |
|---|---|---|
| Girl's | 2, 1 | 4, 2 |
| Women's | 6, 4 | 3, 5 |

parts.stem: Does Dillard's have a dominant strategy?
choices: No: Women's is best if Nordstrom picks Girl's, Girl's is best if Nordstrom picks Women's
parts.explain: Against Girl's: 6 > 2 (Women's). Against Women's: 4 > 3 (Girl's). The best response changes.

parts.stem: Does Nordstrom have a dominant strategy?
parts.explain: Against Girl's: 2 > 1. Against Women's: 5 > 4. Women's both times.
Nordstrom plays Women's; Dillard's best response is Girl's (4 > 3).

parts.stem: What is Dillard's payoff in the Nash equilibrium?
Dillard's would love the 6 in (Women's, Girl's). Why can't it get there?
choices: Nordstrom would not pick Girl's, since Women's is its dominant strategy
parts.explain: Put yourself in your rival's shoes: Nordstrom always picks Women's.

title: Visa vs. Mastercard
stem:
From the S19 slides. Visa (rows) and Mastercard (columns) each decide, without seeing the other's choice, whether to lower merchant fees. Payoffs: (Visa, Mastercard).

| Visa \ Mastercard | Lower Fee | Maintain Fee |
|---|---|---|
| Lower Fee | 2, 2 | 4, 1 |
| Maintain Fee | 1, 4 | 3, 3 |

parts.stem: What kind of game is this?
parts.explain: Neither sees the other's choice, and it is analyzed as played once.

choices: Lower its fee: it is dominant (2 > 1 and 4 > 3)
Maintain its fee: 3 is better than 2

parts.explain: Both play their dominant strategy Lower.

parts.stem: How much combined payoff do Visa and Mastercard give up in equilibrium compared with both maintaining fees?
Could they collude to maintain fees in a one-shot game?
choices: No: each would have an incentive to defect and lower its fee
parts.explain: Slide p. 36. Defecting from (3, 3) to Lower pays 4.

title: Monitoring the warehouse
stem:
A warehouse manager (Boss, rows) decides whether to monitor; a worker (Employee, columns) decides whether to work or shirk. Payoffs: (Boss, Employee).

| Boss \ Employee | Work | Shirk |
|---|---|---|
| Monitor | 6, 3 | 8, 0 |
| Don't Monitor | 10, 3 | 2, 4 |

parts.stem: Is there a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
choices: No: in every cell one player wants to switch
parts.explain: (Monitor, Work): boss switches to Don't (10 > 6). (Don't, Work): employee shirks (4 > 3). (Don't, Shirk): boss monitors (8 > 2). (Monitor, Shirk): employee works (3 > 0).

parts.stem: With what probability should the boss monitor?
parts.explain: Make the employee indifferent: Work = 3; Shirk = 4(1 - p). 3 = 4 - 4p, p = 0.25.

parts.stem: With what probability should the employee work?
parts.explain: Make the boss indifferent: Monitor = 6q + 8(1 - q) = 8 - 2q; Don't = 10q + 2(1 - q) = 2 + 8q. q = 0.6.

parts.stem: What is the boss's expected payoff in the mixed equilibrium?
parts.explain: With q = 0.6: Monitor = 6(0.6) + 8(0.4) = 6.8 (Don't gives the same).

title: Political ads: Facebook vs. Twitter (Game Theory Exercise Part 1)
stem:
From the professor's Game Theory Exercise (your submitted answers). Facebook and Twitter decide in 2019 whether to ban political ads. Political ads are 0.5% of Facebook's ad revenue ($70B, so $350M) and 0.1% of Twitter's ($3B, so $3M). A firm that does not ban faces a 10% chance of a fine of 4% of ad revenue (expected fine $280M for Facebook, $12M for Twitter). If Twitter bans and Facebook does not, Twitter's political ads go to Facebook. If Facebook bans and Twitter does not, 10% of Facebook's political ad revenue ($35M) goes to Twitter. Payoffs are the change in ad revenue in $ millions. Facebook is on the rows, payoffs (Facebook, Twitter):

| Facebook \ Twitter | Ban | Don't Ban |
|---|---|---|
| Ban | -350, -3 | -350, 23 |
| Don't Ban | -277, -3 | -280, -12 |

parts.stem: How do both firms first view the decision in Part 1?
parts.explain: Each decides without knowing the other's choice.

parts.stem: What is Facebook's expected regulatory fine if it does not ban ($ millions)?
Which firm has a dominant strategy?
parts.explain: Facebook: -277 > -350 and -280 > -350. Twitter's best response changes.
Twitter best-responds to Facebook's dominant Don't Ban with Ban (-3 > -12). It matches 2019.

parts.stem: What is Twitter's payoff in the Nash equilibrium ($ millions)?
parts.explain: Twitter gives up its $3M of political ads.
